overview.title: Dense networks: last-layer and loss recipes
overview.main_topic: What densely connected networks assume, where they are used, and the Keras templates for binary, single-label multiclass, and multilabel classification
overview.central_idea: Dense layers assume no structure among input features (every input connects to every unit), so they suit attribute vectors and serve as the classification/regression head of most networks. The task type determines the last layer and loss: 1 sigmoid unit + binary_crossentropy for binary; N softmax units + categorical_crossentropy (or the sparse version for integer labels) for single-label multiclass; N sigmoid units + binary_crossentropy with k-hot targets for multilabel.
overview.importance: These templates are the most reused code patterns in the book. Getting the last-layer activation and loss mismatched is one of the most common beginner bugs, and this page is the definitive cheat sheet.
learning_objectives: Explain why Dense layers suit unstructured vector data and what 'densely connected' means
Choose the last-layer size, activation, and loss for binary, single-label, and multilabel classification
Choose between categorical_crossentropy and sparse_categorical_crossentropy based on label format
Read and write the Functional API templates on the page
Explain why multilabel uses sigmoid rather than softmax
prerequisites: Binary and multiclass examples in chapter 4 (p.130-149)

summary:
Continuing from p.624, densely connected networks **assume no specific structure in the input features**: they are called *densely connected* because each unit of a `Dense` layer is connected to all units of the previous layer, so the layer can model relationships between **any two input features**, unlike a 2D convolution, which only looks at **local** relationships.

They are most commonly used for **categorical/attribute data** (the book cites "the Boston Housing Price dataset used in chapter 4"; chapter 4 actually uses the California Housing dataset, see review flag), and as the **final classification or regression stage** of most networks: chapter 8's ConvNets and chapter 13's recurrent networks typically end with one or two `Dense` layers.

Then three recipes, each written with the Functional API, two hidden `Dense(32, activation="relu")` layers, and the `rmsprop` optimizer:

- **Binary classification**: last layer `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`, loss `binary_crossentropy`, targets 0 or 1.
- **Single-label categorical classification** (exactly one class per sample): `Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax")`; loss `categorical_crossentropy` for one-hot targets or `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` for integer targets.
- **Multilabel categorical classification** (several classes per sample): `Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid")`, loss `binary_crossentropy`, **k-hot encoded** targets. The code for this case starts here and finishes on p.626, where the regression recipe (no activation, `mse` loss) also appears.

The logic: sigmoid gives an independent probability per output; softmax gives a distribution where classes compete; the loss must match the output's probabilistic meaning and the target format.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Dense networks assume no specific structure among input features; every unit of a Dense layer is connected to the units of the previous layer, so the layer can map relationships between any two input features, unlike a 2D convolution, which only looks at local relationships.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each output unit computes a weighted sum over all inputs: $y_j = \operatorname{act}(\sum_i W_{ji} x_i + b_j)$. No pair of inputs is privileged, so feature order does not matter (permuting input columns consistently changes nothing about what can be learned). Note: the book's wording 'connected to every other unit' means every unit in the adjacent layer; units within the same layer are not connected.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This lack of prior is right for tables of attributes but wasteful for images or sequences, where locality is a strong, useful assumption (p.624).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Multilabel: last Dense layer with num_classes units and sigmoid; loss binary_crossentropy; k-hot encoded targets.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each class becomes an independent yes/no question with its own sigmoid probability; binary crossentropy is applied per class and averaged. concepts.name: Densely connected (Dense) layer
concepts.definition: A layer where every input feeds into every unit: $\operatorname{act}(Wx+b)$.
concepts.intuition: Each unit looks at all the features at once, with no notion of neighborhood.
concepts.technical: Parameters: $\text{inputs} \times \text{units} + \text{units}$. No structural prior; models relationships between any two features.
concepts.significance: Default for vector data and the final stage of most networks.
concepts.example: Dense(32, activation="relu") applied to num_input_features attributes.
concepts.misconception: Dense layers are not good image feature extractors compared with convolutions, because they ignore locality.

concepts.name: Matching last-layer activation and loss to the task
concepts.definition: The task type determines the size and activation of the last layer and the loss.
concepts.intuition: The output must have the right probabilistic shape, and the loss must score that shape correctly.
concepts.technical: Binary: 1 sigmoid + binary_crossentropy; single-label: N softmax + (sparse_)categorical_crossentropy; multilabel: N sigmoid + binary_crossentropy; regression: N linear + mse (p.626).
concepts.significance: The core cheat sheet of the page.
concepts.example: Reuters (46 topics, one per article) → Dense(46, softmax).

concepts.name: Softmax output
concepts.definition: Converts N scores into N probabilities summing to 1.
concepts.intuition: Classes compete for a fixed budget of probability.
concepts.misconception: Not appropriate when several labels can be true at once.

concepts.name: Crossentropy losses
concepts.definition: Losses measuring the negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct target(s).
concepts.intuition: Confident wrong predictions are punished heavily; confident right ones cost almost nothing.
concepts.technical: binary_crossentropy for sigmoid outputs (binary or multilabel); categorical_crossentropy for one-hot targets; sparse_categorical_crossentropy for integer targets.
concepts.example: $p=0.9$ on the true class gives loss $\approx 0.105$; $p=0.1$ gives $\approx 2.303$.
concepts.misconception: categorical and sparse_categorical crossentropy are not different objectives; they differ only in target format.

concepts.name: Multilabel classification
concepts.definition: Each sample may belong to several classes; targets are k-hot vectors.
concepts.intuition: N independent yes/no questions answered at once.
concepts.technical: N sigmoid outputs, binary_crossentropy averaged over classes.
concepts.misconception: That output probabilities should sum to 1.

math.title: Sigmoid output and binary crossentropy

variables.meaning: The pre-activation output of the single last unit (a logit).
Predicted probability that the sample belongs to the positive class.
Target, 0 or 1 (the page: 'Your targets should be either 0 or 1').

math.operations: Sigmoid squashes a real number into (0, 1); the loss is the negative log of the probability assigned to the actual target.
math.purpose: Formalizes what the binary classification recipe computes. The book names the activation and loss; the formulas are added here.
math.interpretation: Minimizing BCE is maximum-likelihood estimation of a Bernoulli model of $y$ given $x$.
math.intuition: If $y=1$, loss is $-\log p$: small when $p\to 1$, huge when $p\to 0$.

math.title: Softmax output and categorical crossentropy

variables.meaning: Score (logit) of class $i$ from the last Dense layer.
Index of the true class. sparse_categorical_crossentropy takes $c$ directly as an integer target.

math.operations: Exponentiate and normalize the scores; take the negative log of the true class's probability.
math.purpose: Shows why the two crossentropy variants on the page compute the same quantity and differ only in target format.
math.interpretation: Maximum likelihood for a categorical distribution over exactly one true class.
math.intuition: Raising the true class's score necessarily lowers the others' probabilities: classes compete.
math.numerical_example: Scores $z = (2, 1, 0.1)$ → $p \approx (0.659, 0.242, 0.099)$. If the true class is 0, loss $= -\log 0.659 \approx 0.417$; one-hot target $(1,0,0)$ or integer target $0$ give the same value.

math.title: Multilabel: per-class sigmoid with averaged binary crossentropy

variables.meaning: Entry $i$ of the k-hot target: 1 if class $i$ applies, else 0.
Independent predicted probability that class $i$ applies.

math.operations: Independent sigmoid per output; binary crossentropy per class; mean over classes (Keras averages over the last axis).
math.purpose: Explains the multilabel recipe: N independent binary problems.
math.interpretation: The $p_i$ need not sum to 1; several can be close to 1 simultaneously.
math.intuition: Each output is its own yes/no detector.

code.title: Binary classification template
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(num_input_features,))
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="binary_crossentropy")
code.what_it_does: Builds and compiles a small densely connected binary classifier with the Functional API.

line_explanations.explanation: Import Keras and its layers module.
Symbolic input: each sample is a vector of num_input_features values (batch size left unspecified).
Two hidden Dense layers of 32 units with relu: the representation-learning part.
One unit with sigmoid: outputs the probability of the positive class.
Wrap inputs and outputs into a Model (Functional API).
Compile with the RMSprop optimizer and binary crossentropy loss; targets must be 0 or 1.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: float tensor (batch, num_input_features). Output: (batch, 1) probabilities in (0, 1).
code.algorithm: Forward: two relu affine layers then a sigmoid; training minimizes BCE with RMSprop.
code.theory_link: Sigmoid + BCE is maximum likelihood for a Bernoulli target (see math m1).

parameters.name: num_input_features
parameters.role: Placeholder for the number of features per sample; must be defined before running.

parameters.name: optimizer="rmsprop"
parameters.role: Gradient-descent variant with per-parameter adaptive step sizes.

pitfalls: num_input_features is a placeholder; the snippet does not run until you set it.
Targets must be 0/1 floats or ints, not one-hot pairs.
No metrics are passed to compile(); add metrics=["accuracy"] to monitor accuracy during fit().

code.title: Single-label multiclass classification template
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(num_input_features,))
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="categorical_crossentropy")
code.what_it_does: Same body as the binary template, with a softmax head over num_classes and categorical crossentropy for one-hot targets.

line_explanations.explanation: Input and two hidden relu Dense layers, identical to the binary template.
num_classes units with softmax: a probability distribution over classes.
Build and compile with categorical_crossentropy (one-hot targets). Use loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy" if targets are integers.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: (batch, num_input_features). Output: (batch, num_classes) probabilities summing to 1 per row.
code.algorithm: Softmax regression on top of a learned 2-layer representation, trained by minimizing CCE.
code.theory_link: Softmax + CCE is maximum likelihood for a categorical target (see math m2).

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.role: Number of mutually exclusive classes; sets the output size.

pitfalls: Do not use categorical_crossentropy with integer labels; use sparse_categorical_crossentropy instead.
The hidden width 32 should not be much smaller than num_classes, or it becomes an information bottleneck (p.149).

code.algorithm: N independent logistic outputs on a shared learned representation, trained with mean BCE.
code.theory_link: See math m3: sigmoid per class + binary crossentropy.
pitfalls: Using softmax instead of sigmoid in the (p.626) output layer would force labels to compete.
For prediction, threshold each output (e.g. at 0.5) independently instead of taking an argmax.

deeper.title: Choosing the head: a decision procedure
deeper.body:
Beyond the book's phrasing (but summarizing this page and p.626):
1. Is the target a number (or vector of numbers)? → `Dense(num_values)`, no activation, `mse` (p.626).
2. Is it one yes/no answer? → `Dense(1, "sigmoid")`, `binary_crossentropy`.
3. Exactly one of N classes? → `Dense(N, "softmax")`; one-hot targets → `categorical_crossentropy`, integer targets → `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`.
4. Any subset of N classes? → `Dense(N, "sigmoid")`, `binary_crossentropy`, k-hot targets.

deeper.title: Why softmax fails for multilabel, numerically
deeper.body: Beyond the book: suppose an image truly has 2 of 3 tags. With softmax, the best the model can do is put 0.5 on each correct tag, so each correct tag's probability is capped at 0.5 and gets confused with uncertainty. With 3 sigmoids, the model can output (0.95, 0.95, 0.02), expressing confident presence of both tags.

deeper.title: Dense heads on top of other architectures
deeper.body: As the page says, ConvNets (chapter 8) and recurrent networks (chapter 13) usually end with Dense layers. The same head recipes apply unchanged: e.g. a ConvNet for 10-way digit classification ends with `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` and, with integer labels, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (as on p.258).

takeaways: Dense layers assume no structure among input features; they model relationships between any pair of features.
Dense networks handle attribute vectors and form the classification/regression head of most networks.
Single-label multiclass: Dense(N, softmax) + categorical_crossentropy (one-hot) or sparse_categorical_crossentropy (integers).
Multilabel: Dense(N, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy, k-hot targets.

questions.question: Your labels are integers from 0 to 9, each sample has exactly one class. Which last layer and loss does the page prescribe?
questions.explanation: Single-label → softmax over num_classes; integer targets → sparse version. Sigmoid + BCE is the multilabel recipe; Dense(1, sigmoid) is binary; categorical_crossentropy expects one-hot targets, not integers.

questions.question: A document can be tagged with any subset of 20 topics. Which configuration fits?
questions.explanation: This is the multilabel recipe on the page. Softmax forces topics to compete; a single sigmoid unit answers only one yes/no question; mse with no activation is the regression recipe (p.626).

questions.question: Why does the page say Dense layers are unlike 2D convolution layers?
questions.answer: A Dense layer connects every input to every unit, so it can map relationships between any two input features and assumes no structure; a 2D convolution only looks at local relationships (nearby pixels).
questions.explanation: This is the architecture-prior idea from p.624 applied to Dense vs Conv2D.

questions.question: A binary classifier outputs $p = 0.8$ for a sample whose target is $y = 0$. What is the binary crossentropy loss? What would it be if $y=1$?
questions.explanation: BCE $= -[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$; only the term for the actual target remains.

questions.question: Besides processing attribute vectors, what other role do Dense layers play according to the page?
questions.answer: They form the final classification or regression stage of most networks, e.g. ConvNets (chapter 8) and recurrent networks (chapter 13) typically end with one or two Dense layers.

questions.question: The page cites 'the Boston Housing Price dataset used in chapter 4'. What dataset does chapter 4 of this edition actually use, and what kind of task is it?
questions.answer: The California Housing Price dataset (section 4.3.1), a regression task predicting house prices from numerical features.
questions.explanation: See p.150; the Boston reference seems to be carried over from the previous edition.

questions.question: Without looking, write the four-line 'head + compile' for binary, single-label, and multilabel classification. Check against the page.
questions.answer: Binary: Dense(1, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy. Single-label: Dense(num_classes, softmax) + categorical_crossentropy (or sparse_...). Multilabel: Dense(num_classes, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy.
